advisor.summary: A proprietor deducting business use of a personal vehicle picks between the standard mileage rate — 72.5 cents per mile for the first half of 2026, raised to 76 cents for miles driven July through December — and actual expenses multiplied by the business-use percentage. The choice is stickier than clients expect: Rev. Proc. 2019-46 requires electing the standard rate in the vehicle's first business year to preserve later flexibility, and claiming accelerated depreciation in year one locks the vehicle into actual expenses for life. Under either method the deduction stands or falls on a §274(d) contemporaneous mileage log. The engine applies the advisor-computed incremental deduction — the margin of the better method over the current baseline — as an entity deduction; the method comparison itself is workpaper arithmetic.
mechanics: The standard rate folds depreciation, fuel, insurance, and repairs into a single per-mile figure — 72.5 cents for January through June 2026 and 76 cents for July through December under the IRS's mid-year adjustment — with parking and tolls deductible on top; it is unavailable to fleets of five or more simultaneous vehicles or after accelerated depreciation has been claimed.

The actual method deducts operating costs plus depreciation, multiplied by the business-use percentage (business miles over total miles), with the §280F luxury-auto caps metering depreciation on passenger vehicles.

Rev. Proc. 2019-46 supplies the sequencing rule: electing standard mileage in year one deems depreciation straight-line and preserves the right to alternate later, while claiming MACRS, first-year expensing, or bonus in year one permanently forecloses the standard rate for that vehicle.
The standard rate's per-mile depreciation component reduces basis every year, so long-time standard-rate users encounter unexpected gain at sale or trade-in.

§274(d) strict substantiation controls: date, mileage, destination, and business purpose recorded at or near the time — reconstructed logs and estimates fail, and commuting to a regular work location is never business mileage (a qualifying home office converts home-to-client trips).
The model deducts the advisor-computed incremental benefit of the better method over the client's current practice; the comparison worksheet — not the model — selects the method.

requirements: A contemporaneous mileage log — app, diary, or spreadsheet — whichever method applies.
Standard rate: election made in the vehicle's first business year, with fewer than five vehicles in simultaneous use.
Actual method: expense receipts and a defensible business-use percentage.
risks: The absent log is the leading audit theory: §274(d) mileage ranks among the most commonly disallowed deductions on exam, and Sanford v. Commissioner forecloses the estimate that might rescue it — the app costs less than the adjustment.
Defaulting into actual-plus-accelerated in year one permanently forecloses the standard rate for that vehicle; the first-year decision deserves a worksheet, not a habit.
Near-100-percent business-use claims on a household's only vehicle invite scrutiny, and miscounted commuting is the recurring adjustment.
Standard-rate depreciation quietly erodes basis — expect taxable gain at trade-in after years on the rate.
If business use of a MACRS-depreciated vehicle falls to half or below, §280F recaptures the excess over straight line.
stateNotes: Conformity: the deduction rides inside federal business income, so conforming states absorb it without adjustment; states publish no separate mileage rates for this purpose.

PTET interaction: for entity owners the economics run through an accountable-plan reimbursement, which reduces electing-entity income before any pass-through entity tax; a Schedule C filer has no PTET interaction.
Missouri: conforms through its federal starting point (RSMo §143.121); the Missouri return simply carries the reduced business income.
reviewChecklist: Log method in place and generating contemporaneous entries — sample-checked, never assumed.
First-business-year vehicles: both methods projected over the expected holding period before filing.
Modeled incremental deduction tied to the actual comparison worksheet.
Cumulative standard-rate depreciation carried against basis in the permanent file.
Entity-owner vehicles reimbursed through an accountable plan rather than deducted personally.

client.teaser: There are two ways to deduct the same driving — we pick the one that pays more.
client.headline: Make every business mile pay off
plainEnglish: When you drive your own car for business, the IRS gives you two ways to deduct it. The simple way pays a flat rate per business mile — 72.5 cents early in 2026, then 76 cents for the second half of the year. The detailed way deducts the business share of what the car truly costs: gas, insurance, repairs, and wear.

Which one wins depends on your car and your driving. Lots of miles in a thrifty car favors the flat rate. A pricey car driven less favors actual costs. The first-year choice can lock you in, so it pays to do the math up front.
Every option needs one thing: a record of your business trips. A phone app does this automatically. That record is the difference between a deduction that survives questions and one that disappears.
client.analogy: It is like choosing between a flat per-mile reimbursement and an expense report. Same trips, two ways to count them — we run both and hand you the bigger number.
benefits: Turns the driving you already do into a real deduction
Cuts income tax and self-employment tax for sole proprietors
We run the comparison both ways so nothing is left on the table
A phone app makes record-keeping nearly effortless
